G7 leaders are gathering in Évian today to discuss energy security, AI, and critical minerals.
 
One question stays with me: Can countries make the right development choices before infrastructure is locked in?
 
I have come to see energy modelling not as a technical exercise, but as a way to inform decisions before they become irreversible. Without integrated planning, countries risk fuel import dependence, grid congestion, stranded assets, and missed jobs. With it, energy systems can be designed for industrialization, resilience, and inclusive growth from the start.
 
Three takeaways stand out:
 
🔹 Model demand and risk at subnational scale.
With more than 1,000 active Earth observation satellites, a tenfold rise in publicly available Earth observation data in a decade, and over 500 machine-learning-ready geospatial datasets, governments can now model demand growth, climate risk, and system constraints below the national level. That means infrastructure can go where it is most resilient, affordable, and impactful.
 
🔹 Link energy decisions to real development outcomes.
The transition is full of trade-offs: cost and resilience, speed and equity, access and industrial growth. Integrated models help countries test scenarios side by side, asking not only what is cheapest, but what is most robust under climate shocks, what reduces fuel imports, and what creates the most jobs per dollar invested. Complexity becomes a set of choices governments can act on.
 
🔹 Align governments and finance around one evidence base.
When planning ministries, utilities, finance ministries, and regulators work from the same models, coordination improves. Pipelines become clearer. Policy becomes more coherent. Finance becomes easier to mobilize. Modelling becomes a common language linking national plans, climate commitments, and investment decisions into one credible framework.
 
The conversations in Évian will shape the global energy agenda. But the deeper test is whether every country, not only the G7, can shape its own future with the same foresight. 
 
Energy modelling is no longer an add-on. It is strategic infrastructure. And it decides whether a country locks in vulnerability or builds lasting resilience.
